sections.h2: How did Ann Arbor's history shape the housing a seller has today?
sections.html:
In 1956 voters merged the city of East Ann Arbor into Ann Arbor, and the current City Hall opened in 1963 after a 1960 bond vote. The 1960s and 1970s brought a reputation for student activism, including the first U.S. teach-in against the Vietnam War in 1965, and the Human Rights Party won council seats on the student vote in the early 1970s.

Ann Arbor began as a land speculators' plat registered with Wayne County in 1824 and grew around two anchors: the county seat, awarded in 1827, and the University of Michigan, which took over land first offered to the state as a capitol site. The city lost that capitol bid to Lansing, accepted the university in 1837, and incorporated as a city in 1851.

Long before that, Anishinaabe peoples lived and traveled through the area, and the land was ceded to the United States under the 1807 Treaty of Detroit. The Huron River gives the city its hilly shape. Elevation runs from about 750 feet along the water to 1,015 feet on the west side, which is why houses on the slopes have different drainage, views and basements than those on flat ground.

The Tree Town nickname rests on 50,000 trees along streets and as many again in parks. Emerald ash borers have killed many of the city's roughly 10,500 ash trees, a fact worth knowing if a mature ash stands near your house or the sewer line.

sections.h2: Why is the Ann Arbor housing market unlike most of Michigan?
sections.html:
Renters, graduate students and short stays drive much of the market, and prices sit far above state norms. Owning a typical home costs $2,436 a month with a mortgage, compared with a $1,649 median rent.

About one resident in three had a different address a year earlier, and 18.6 percent were born abroad. Because owners live in fewer than half of homes, many houses are rentals, and prospective buyers will raise licensing early.

sections.h2: What does the University of Michigan mean for an Ann Arbor seller?
sections.html:
It means a deep, stable pool of employed buyers and renters. The university employs about 30,000 people, roughly 12,000 of them at the medical center, and research money brings in technology firms, labs and startups.

The technology history goes back to the 1930s, when the Kadette radio was made here. Today the list includes Duo Security, a KLA North American headquarters that opened in 2021, a regional Google office, Internet2 and Merit Network, and more than twenty video game and XR studios. Federal sites add to the base, among them a NOAA Great Lakes laboratory and an EPA vehicle emissions laboratory. Auto firms such as General Motors and Visteon also employ residents.

Census figures show 77.9 percent of adults with a bachelor's degree and a 20.0 minute average commute, and about 36 percent of 2019 trips were on foot, by bike or on transit.

sections.h2: Which roads, parks and schools matter when you list an Ann Arbor house?
sections.html:
Buyers check three things: how a house connects to the freeways, whether it sits near parks, and which high school it feeds.

  • US-23 hugs the east side, M-14 the north and I-94 the south and west, while Michigan Avenue, Washtenaw Avenue and Ford Road carry cross-town traffic.
  • TheRide runs buses across the city and into Ypsilanti, and Amtrak's Wolverine stops at the Ann Arbor station.
  • More than 160 parks include Buhr Park, Fuller Recreation Area and a 30,000 square foot skatepark that opened in 2014 inside Veterans Memorial Park.
  • Ann Arbor Public Schools had 17,070 students in 2021 to 2022 and runs Pioneer, Huron, Skyline and Community high schools, with a well-known music program.

Private and charter choices include Greenhills School, Clonlara School and Michigan Islamic Academy. The Border-to-Border Trail links the city with Ypsilanti along the river for walkers and cyclists, and photos of it sell houses nearby.

sections.h2: What does Ann Arbor's weather mean for a house?
sections.html:
Winters are cold and snowy, with January highs near 32 degrees and snowfall of about 61 inches a season, normally from November to April. Summers are warm and humid, with July highs around 84 degrees and 10 days at or above 90. Precipitation totals about 38 inches a year, heaviest in summer.

Those numbers matter to a buyer's inspector. Roofs, gutters, basement walls and sump pumps carry the load in a place with this much snow and rain, so gather receipts for roof and drainage work before you list. Ask any serious buyer whether they plan an inspection, and offer your repair records up front.

sections.h2: Can a buyer run a short-term rental in an Ann Arbor house?
sections.html:
Only with a city license, and the zoning rules narrow who can get one. Chapter 97 of the city code covers stays of 30 consecutive days or fewer, and the license costs $500 per unit each year.

  • In zones whose names begin with R, only the owner's principal residence can qualify, backed by a sworn statement of principal residency.
  • Accessory dwelling units cannot be short-term rentals.
  • Companies acting for an owner cannot hold a license, and neither can a tenant who never moved in.
  • A non-owner-occupied property in a zone that permits one needs a valid Certificate of Compliance first.
  • Apply and pay through the city's STREAM portal. Review takes up to 21 business days, denied applications are not refunded, and the license renews yearly.

Some investors picture a vacation rental and then learn the zone forbids it. For long-term renting, the city runs a Green Rental Housing program with a HERS energy score of 110 or lower as its pass mark.

sections.h2: How do Ann Arbor assessments, appeals and transfers work?
sections.html:
The Assessor's Office on the fifth floor of Larcom City Hall, 301 E. Huron St., takes the transfer affidavit and the exemption forms in person, by mail or through the city's online submission page, and answers at 734.794.6530. New owners file the Property Transfer Affidavit within 45 days, and sellers rescind their own principal residence exemption on the old home.

Property tax supplies more than half of city revenue. Taxable value moves each year by the inflation multiplier or 5 percent, whichever is lower, and a sale lifts it back toward assessed value. Notices go out in early March, and the Board of Review sits for four days beginning the Monday of the third week of March. A residential owner who is turned down there has until July 31 to go to the Michigan Tax Tribunal.

sections.h2: What does recording a deed cost for an Ann Arbor property?
sections.html:
Washtenaw County has fewer than 2,000,000 residents, so the county tax is 55 cents per $500 and the state tax is $3.75 per $500. A $450,000 house owes $3,870 at recording, and the seller pays. State law sets the recording fee at $30 per document, but a charter county may set its own, so ask the Washtenaw County Register of Deeds for its table.

Warranty deeds need a county treasurer tax certificate. Exemptions cover transfers under $100, gifts from parent to child or grandparent to grandchild, and court-ordered transfers that set no price.

faqs.q: Do owners or renters hold most Ann Arbor homes?
faqs.a: Renters hold the larger share. The Census Bureau puts the owner-occupied rate at 45.5 percent for 2020 to 2024.

faqs.q: How long does the short-term rental review take in Ann Arbor?
faqs.a: Up to 21 business days after the $500 payment. Applications go through the city's STREAM portal.

faqs.q: What is the combined transfer tax on a $450,000 Ann Arbor sale?
faqs.a: It is $3,870, from $8.60 per $1,000. The seller pays it when the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Where do I file sale paperwork with the Ann Arbor assessor?
faqs.a: Larcom City Hall, fifth floor, 301 E. Huron St., or online. The office is reachable at 734.794.6530.

faqs.q: How snowy are Ann Arbor winters?
faqs.a: Snowfall averages about 61 inches a season, falling mostly from November to April, and January highs sit near 32 degrees.
